parts.title: Children's literature studies today
parts.article:
Children’s literature studies today
 
(A) Who studies children’s literature and what is it that they study? The answers to this question are complex and messy, because of the many confounding factors which exist in this field.
 
(B) Firstly, unlike literature for adults, children’s literature is not generally written by its own readers. Adults write for children, and thus adult perceptions of what children are and of what they could and should become are woven into the literature.
 
(C) Furthermore, some of those who study children’s literature (and those who write certain kinds of children’s books) are less interested in literary values than in the kinds of lessons it can teach- either in terms of creating better children or in terms of serving a particular curriculum. The issue of how a teacher can use a children’s book is often contentious, but even outside the classroom, much material for children is still didactic.
 
(D) Thirdly, while almost all literature is currently promoted within a strong commercial matrix, children’s literature is often especially targeted for marketing initiatives. This fact means that readers are often recruited with a message that is negligibly literary and significantly oriented to ideas of consumption. Daniel Hade (2002) has raised useful questions about whether children’s experience of reading is altered when their books are part of a larger marketing framework involving the movie, the game, and the toy of a popular children’s book. How children perceive and respond to their stories in this new context is an important question.
 
(E) It is also important to note that texts in an ever-increasing range of new media compete with print media for the attention of the child reader, and create definitional issues for scholars. Does the term literature’ exclusively imply a verbal text? If not, where are the limits? Could a literary computer game ever be considered a work of literature? If not, what kind of attention should be paid to it, since children themselves undoubtedly perceive their print literature as part of a broader continuum? The internet provides one forum through which children now communicate with each other. (In 2003, the internet search engine Google listed 7,920,000 sites relating to the Harry Potter novels; even allowing for duplication and dead ends, that is a number with revolutionary implications.)
 
(F) Finally, in the context of the higher education institutions where the formal study of children’s literature is often located, at least three disciplinary frameworks (English, education, and librarianship) fragment the focus of scholarly study of children’s literature. How is the value of the imaginative encounter with the work of literature sustained and honored among such a welter of conflicting interests? One route through this maze is to ask the child readers for help. As David Lewis (2001) has perceptively noted, what children think of reading is not usually the same as what adults think, whether teachers or parents. As Lewis points out, children ‘sometimes see more and they often see differently’. If those who study reading can explore children’s perceptions as well as those of adults, their understanding of the nature of reading will be enhanced.
 
(G) Lewis makes a further valid point when he adds that exploring children’s perceptions is usually justified for educational reasons: “It is true that a better understanding of how children read and how they learn to read, is a prerequisite to improved approaches to teaching. However, it can also be argued, as Lewis rightly does, that when children’s responses to literature are accessed and interpreted, they frequently lead to an understanding of how picture books appeal to children.
 
(H) Young people’s accounts of what and how they read also enable a more sophisticated description of many of the complex processes involved in reading. All descriptions of reading runs the risk of solipsism: i.e. this is how I read so this is what reading is for everyone. Asking other readers how they read, however, reduces that risk. For example, if I am a strong visualizer as I read, I may consider that visualization is a key component of successful reading and I may judge books by their capacity to evoke a vivid visual response. Other readers, however, may help me to realize that not everyone reads with mental pictures. Some readers respond to the patterns of the words, ‘hearing’ them inaudibly like a subliminal radio program. Others respond to the patterns of feelings in the story, responding with an emotional connection. Talking to competent readers, of all ages, provides a better understanding of reading experiences.
 
(I) Children’s insights are even more important when it comes to understanding the significance of print literature as one aspect of literary culture. Too often adults assume that reading any book at all is a more worthwhile experience than playing a digital game of any kind. A humbler approach would include asking why the game appeals to the player. Many adults will probably never develop the automatic skills to process a game as readily as they can read a book. This does not indicate that a book is better, but that a particular set of skills is absent. Non-players must acknowledge that some fictional universes are thus closed to them, and a logical response would be to find someone who can guide them to the pleasures and challenges of the gaming world. Games need to be judged individually just as books do, and any evaluative framework needs to take this into account.

Q27 Which of the following best summarises the writer’s argument in the second paragraph?

  • A Children are portrayed as adults see them.
  • B Children are unable to write their own stories.
  • C Adults fail to stimulate children’s imaginations.
  • D Adult literature is too difficult for children.

Q28 In the third paragraph, what does the writer say is the main interest of some people who study children’s literature?

  • A the quality of the writing
  • B the imaginative content of stories
  • C the instructive nature of children’s books
  • D the way children are written about in stories

Q29 The main point of the writer’s argument in the fifth paragraph is to

  • A demonstrate that academics consider computer games to be a logical extension of children’s literature.
  • B explore the impact of computers on the boundaries of children’s literature.
  • C illustrate that literature and computer games have different origins.
  • D prove that children are using computers more than they are reading literature.

reference:
Q27

干扰 你可能想选B（儿童不能自己写故事），但这只是引出成人代笔这一现象的客观事实，作者真正想强调的是成人视角对作品的实质性渗透。

句子 第2段："Firstly, unlike literature for adults, children's literature is not generally written by its own readers. Adults write for children, and thus adult perceptions of what children are and of what they could and should become are woven into the literature."

解析 第二段的核心观点是，儿童文学是由成年人写的，因此成年人对儿童的看法和期望（即成人眼中的儿童形象）被深深编织进了文学作品中。

Q28

解析 第三段明确指出，许多研究者更关心儿童文学能教给孩子什么“道理或课程”（lessons it can teach/didactic），也就是它的教育或说教性质，而不是它的文学价值。

干扰 你可能会因为看到“literary values”去选A（写作质量），但原文明确用了“less interested in”（没那么感兴趣）来直接否定了这个方向。

句子 第3段："Furthermore, some of those who study children's literature... are less interested in literary values than in the kinds of lessons it can teach- either in terms of creating better children or in terms of serving a particular curriculum. ... much material for children is still didactic."

Q29

解析 第五段的核心在于提出了一系列问题，探讨了新媒体和电脑游戏如何冲击并模糊了儿童文学的“定义边界（definitional issues/limits）”。

干扰 你可能想选A（学者认为电脑游戏是文学的逻辑延伸），但作者这里只是一直在“提出问题”探讨边界，并没有直接给出学者已经完全认定它是延伸的肯定结论。

句子 第5段："It is also important to note that texts in an ever-increasing range of new media compete with print media for the attention of the child reader, and create definitional issues for scholars. Does the term literature' exclusively imply a verbal text? If not, where are the limits? Could a literary computer game ever be considered a work of literature?"

Q30

句子 第5段："...what kind of attention should be paid to it, since children themselves undoubtedly perceive their print literature as part of a broader continuum?"

解析 原文说儿童无疑将印刷文学视为一个“更广阔连续体的一部分”（broader continuum），这意味着他们并没有把两者割裂开来，与题干的“清晰区分（clear distinction）”完全相反。

干扰 看到“undoubtedly”（毫无疑问）不要就急着选YES，要看清后面的宾语意思是“连续、不分割的整体”，这恰恰反驳了题目的“明确区分”。

Q31

解析 原文明确指出在高等教育机构中，儿童文学研究被至少“三种学科框架”（three disciplinary frameworks）所分割，这直接否定了题干所说的“仅限于一个学科领域（restricted to one subject area）”。

干扰 原文中的“fragment”（使碎片化/分割）和“至少三个学科”直接打脸了题干里的“restricted to one”（限制于一个）。

句子 第6段："Finally, in the context of the higher education institutions where the formal study of children's literature is often located, at least three disciplinary frameworks (English, education, and librarianship) fragment the focus of scholarly study of children's literature."

Q32

解析 文中确实提到了探索儿童的阅读感知有助于改进教学方法、理解图画书的吸引力，但通篇根本没有提到这是否能“帮助父母为孩子挑选合适的书（assist parents to choose suitable books）”。

干扰 你可能根据生活常识觉得了解孩子喜好肯定有助于挑书，但只要文章没明确写出“父母选书”这个具体行为，就必须坚决选 NOT GIVEN。

句子 第8段："It is true that a better understanding of how children read and how they learn to read, is a prerequisite to improved approaches to teaching. However, it can also be argued... they frequently lead to an understanding of how picture books appeal to children."

Q33

解析 原文明确表示，当获取并解读了孩子们对文学的反应时（即获得更多孩子如何阅读的信息），这通常能让人更好地理解图画书为何对孩子有吸引力。

干扰 题干中的“illustrated stories”（带插图的故事）就是原文“picture books”（图画书）的完美同义替换，前后逻辑因果完全一致。

句子 第8段："...when children's responses to literature are accessed and interpreted, they frequently lead to an understanding of how picture books appeal to children."

Q34

干扰 千万不要把“问游戏为什么好玩”主观脑补延伸成“问孩子想要增加什么新功能”，这种无中生有的细节描写就是经典的 NOT GIVEN。

句子 第10段："A humbler approach would include asking why the game appeals to the player."

解析 原文只建议大人应该采取谦虚的态度，去问孩子“为什么这个游戏吸引你（why the game appeals to the player）”，但完全没有提到应该去问孩子“希望游戏包含哪些新功能/特征（features they would like... to include）”。

Q35

解析 题干问年轻人讲述自己如何阅读能带来什么，原文说这能让我们对阅读中许多复杂的过程序述得更加成熟精细，即“深入了解阅读的复杂性（intricacies）”。

干扰 选项中的“intricacies”（错综复杂的事物）完美对应了原文的“complex processes”（复杂过程），直接定位替换即可得分。

句子 第9段："Young people's accounts of what and how they read also enable a more sophisticated description of many of the complex processes involved in reading."

Q36

解析 题干问如何降低唯我论（认为别人都和自己一样）的风险，原文直接给出对策：“去问其他读者他们是怎么阅读的”，也就是去发现别人使用的阅读技巧。

干扰 只要找到“reduces that risk”往前看依据，就能精准锁定“Asking other readers how they read”，它与选项C的意思完全吻合。

句子 第9段："All descriptions of reading runs the risk of solipsism: i.e. this is how I read so this is what reading is for everyone. Asking other readers how they read, however, reduces that risk."

Q37

句子 第9段："For example, if I am a strong visualizer as I read, I may consider that visualization is a key component of successful reading and I may judge books by their capacity to evoke a vivid visual response."

解析 原文说如果我是一个强大的视觉化读者，我会根据书本能否唤起生动的视觉反应（evoke a vivid visual response）来评判它，这对应的就是“在脑海中产生各种图像”。

干扰 原文的“visual response”（视觉反应）在选项中被直白地同义替换成了“images in their minds”（脑海中的图像），寻找视觉相关词汇即可。

Q38

解析 第10段强调儿童的洞见对于我们理解“印刷文学只是文学文化的一个方面”很重要，大人应该打破偏见，承认游戏和书一样需要被单独评价，即接受文学在今天以多种形式存在。

干扰 做这题不能只看单句，要结合本段探讨将“数字游戏”也纳入评价框架的语境，从而顺理成章地得出文学存在于“多种形式（variety of forms）”中的结论。

句子 第10段："Children's insights are even more important when it comes to understanding the significance of print literature as one aspect of literary culture. Too often adults assume that reading any book at all is a more worthwhile experience than playing a digital game of any kind."

Q39

解析 题干问大人读书比玩游戏容易说明了什么，原文明确指出这绝不代表书更好，而仅仅是因为大人“缺乏某套特定的技能（a particular set of skills is absent）”。

干扰 原文的“is absent”（不存在/缺失）直接同义替换了选项中的“the lack of”（缺乏），非常直白对应。

句子 第10段："Many adults will probably never develop the automatic skills to process a game as readily as they can read a book. This does not indicate that a book is better, but that a particular set of skills is absent."

Q40

解析 文章前半部分详细回顾了儿童文学研究领域面临的各种混乱和挑战，后半部分则指明了出路——提出“向小读者求助”、“纳入游戏评价框架”等如何继续推进研究的建设性建议。

干扰 你可能想选B（讨论商业影响），但商业化只是文章众多挑战中的冰山一角，不足以概括全篇“提出各种问题 + 指明解决路径”的宏大主旨结构。

句子 全文结构。第1段指出答案是“complex and messy”（复杂且混乱的），接着第2至6段详述挑战（成人视角代入、过度说教、被商业营销裹挟、新媒体定义冲击、学科边界碎片化）；第7段笔锋一转：“One route through this maze is to ask the child readers for help.”，并在随后段落提出推进建议。
